strengths: The paper addresses an identifiable audience in visual robustness, representation learning, and computational neuroscience. Its per-orientation heatmaps reveal structured successes and failures that average OoD accuracy would conceal, making the descriptive findings useful.

The experimental coverage is substantial: three object categories, including asymmetric Shepard–Metzler objects; three architectures; different training orientation ranges; cross-category transfer; pretraining; and rotation augmentation. Keeping training-set size constant and repeating experiments with five instance selections are useful controls.

The small-angle, in-plane, and silhouette components provide an interpretable account of the observed accuracy patterns. The main figures explain the learning paradigm effectively, and the neural visualizations motivate a plausible shared-feature hypothesis. A code and data link is supplied.
weaknesses: Necessary: The central mechanistic claims exceed the evidence. Figures 4 and S.7 show associations between activation similarity and accuracy, and between fully-seen and partially-seen invariance scores. These associations do not establish that particular shared neurons cause transfer, or that invariance develops in the proposed direction. Shared visual similarity could contribute to both measurements. A targeted intervention with matched controls could strengthen this attribution; alternatively, the abstract and discussion should consistently present dissemination as a hypothesis supported by correlational evidence. The claimed correspondence with biological mechanisms also needs qualification.

Necessary: Predictive validation of the geometric model is unclear. Section 4.2 fits the logistic parameters by optimizing Pearson correlation with measured network accuracy, but no separate evaluation data are specified for the correlations in Figures 3 and S.5. Clarify which conditions share fitted parameters and evaluate independent orientations, runs, or conditions if retaining claims of predictive power; otherwise describe the results as descriptive fits. Because the generalizable/non-generalizable partition is derived from this accuracy-fitted model, the accuracy separation in Figure S.6 provides limited independent confirmation.

Necessary: The invariance measure needs stronger validation before supporting the proposed explanation. Equations 5–7 compare region-averaged activations, so a strongly orientation-selective neuron can receive perfect invariance when two regions happen to have equal means. Retaining only unit–instance pairs whose mean activity exceeds the threshold in both regions can further favor similar responses and change the evaluated population. Report retained-pair counts and check whether the findings survive an analysis of individual orientations, independent selection of units, and reasonable changes to the activity and partition thresholds.

Necessary: Important evaluation details are missing from the manuscript. Section 4.4 specifies training-set size but does not adequately specify evaluation render counts, orientation-bin resolution, or sampling within bins. Learning rates are selected using OoD stability without a stated validation/test separation. The error-bar definitions and aggregation underlying the neural scatter plots also need clarification. These details are needed to assess the reliability and reproduce the quantitative findings.

Optional strengthening: Keep a fixed cohort of partially-seen test instances while varying the fully-seen training sources, and include a zero-fully-seen baseline. Currently, increasing fully-seen instances from 10 to 40 also reduces partially-seen instances from 40 to 10. A fixed target cohort would help distinguish source-diversity effects from changes in target composition and class competition, especially in cross-category experiments.
